anchorData: FENCE: exactly 40 m of wire for a rectangular vegetable plot (sukuma wiki and spinach) beside the house, so 2(length + width) = 40 and length + width = 20 m. Let width = x m, then length = (20 − x) m and area A = x(20 − x) = 20x − x² (m²). Valid widths: 0 < x < 20 (at x = 20 the length is 0, so no plot; above 20 the length is negative, which is impossible). AREA TABLE (width x | length 20−x | area): 2 | 18 | 36; 4 | 16 | 64; 5 | 15 | 75; 6 | 14 | 84; 8 | 12 | 96; 10 | 10 | 100; 12 | 8 | 96; 14 | 6 | 84; 15 | 5 | 75; 16 | 4 | 64; 18 | 2 | 36; 20 | 0 | 0 (no plot). KEY FACTS: x = 8 and x = 12 both give 96 m²; x = 10 gives the maximum area of 100 m² (a 10 m by 10 m square); areas are symmetric about x = 10 (x = 6 and x = 14 both give 84; x = 4 and 16 both give 64). Target-area equation: x(20 − x) = 96 becomes x² − 20x + 96 = 0 = (x − 8)(x − 12), because 8 + 12 = 20 and 8 × 12 = 96. Maximum form: A = 100 − (x − 10)², so A ≤ 100. Square checks for L2: 12² = (10 + 2)² = 144; 8² = (10 − 2)² = 64; 10² = 100. L3 mental calculation: 52² − 48² = (52 − 48)(52 + 48) = 4 × 100 = 400 (2704 − 2304 = 400). L1 expansions: x(20 − x) = 20x − x²; (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15. L5 factorisation: 2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3); grouping uses ac = 6 and the numbers 6 and 1: 2x² + 6x + x + 3. L7 situations: (a) MANDAZI TRAY: 60 mandazi in a rectangle of x rows and (x + 4) columns, so x(x + 4) = 60, x² + 4x − 60 = 0, (x + 10)(x − 6) = 0, x = 6 (x = −10 rejected), giving 6 rows of 10 mandazi. (b) PATH AROUND SHAMBA: shamba 12 m by 8 m (96 m²), path of uniform width w m all around the outside, total area shamba plus path = 140 m², so (12 + 2w)(8 + 2w) = 140, w² + 10w − 11 = 0, (w + 11)(w − 1) = 0, w = 1 m (w = −11 rejected), giving outer size 14 m by 10 m = 140 m². (c) THROWN BALL: height h = 20t − 5t² metres after t seconds (model with g taken as 10 m/s²). h = 0 gives t = 0 and t = 4. h = 15 gives t² − 4t + 3 = 0, (t − 1)(t − 3) = 0, t = 1 s (rising) and t = 3 s (falling); check 20 − 5 = 15 and 60 − 45 = 15. L8 design task: 40 m fence, target area 84 m², x² − 20x + 84 = 0, (x − 6)(x − 14) = 0, giving a 6 m by 14 m plot. Impossible target: 105 m² is more than 100 m², so no plot exists.
characters: MAMA WANJIRU: a farmer in Kericho with exactly 40 m of fencing wire for a rectangular vegetable plot beside her house (sukuma wiki and spinach). Her children CHEBET and KIPROP try different widths and discover the equal areas (8 m and 12 m both give 96 m²). Kericho: the setting for the phenomenon (tea country, Rift Valley highlands). Learners model the plot with string loops (40 m scaled, e.g. 40 cm loops with 1 cm = 1 m), grid paper and area tiles (x² tile, x strip, unit square). Other contexts: a mandazi tray at a Kisumu market stall (L7), a 12 m by 8 m shamba with a path around it in the Rift Valley (L7), a football kicked at Kasarani (L7), and a school garden for the learners' own school (L8). The class uses a Driving Question Board (DQB) and a cumulative model that grows each lesson.
outcome: With 40 m of wire the length is 20 − x, so the area is x(20 − x). Setting this equal to 96 gives x² − 20x + 96 = 0, which factorises as (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, so x = 8 and x = 12 both work. These are the same 8 m by 12 m rectangle with width and length swapped (the width and length add up to 20 m, so the pattern is symmetric about x = 10). The area is greatest, 100 m², at x = 10 because A = 100 − (x − 10)², and a square can never be less than 0, so no area above 100 m² is possible.
conventions: x = width in metres; length = (20 − x) m; area in m² (square metres). Perimeter is fixed at 40 m throughout. The plots with widths 8 m and 12 m are the same rectangle (8 m by 12 m) turned round, NOT two different shapes; lessons must say this plainly. Different-looking shapes with equal area would have different perimeters (e.g. 4 m by 24 m also has area 96 m² but needs 56 m of wire), so with a fixed fence the only equal-area pair is x and 20 − x. Vocabulary: quadratic expression (highest power 2, e.g. 20x − x²); quadratic equation (expression = 0, e.g. x² − 20x + 96 = 0); identity (true for all values); factorise (write as a product); root or solution. Identities named exactly as: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). Write the standard form as ax² + bx + c = 0. Use the zero-product property: if p × q = 0 then p = 0 or q = 0. Always check solutions against the context (lengths must be positive, 0 < x < 20). Use the minus sign − and × for multiplication. Methods named: sum-and-product method (x² + bx + c), grouping method and area-tile method (ax² + bx + c). Cumulative model: v1 area models (L2), all three identities (L3), two solutions (L6), final model with maximum (L8). Do not use completing the square or the quadratic formula as taught methods (outside this sub-strand scope); L8 only shows A = 100 − (x − 10)² as an identity check using L2 and L3.

lessonMap.teaches: Write a width × length area as an algebraic expression and expand it to see an x² term (e.g. x(20 − x) = 20x − x² and (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15), recognising this as a quadratic expression
lessonMap.buildsOn: None (launches the phenomenon); uses Grade 9 expansion of simple brackets and area of rectangles
lessonMap.usesData: Fence 40 m, length = 20 − x, the area table (predict, then check), the 8 m and 12 m plots both 96 m², 10 m giving 100 m², widths above 20 m impossible; expansions x(20 − x) and (x + 3)(x + 5)

lessonMap.focus: Deriving the squares identities from area
lessonMap.teaches: Derive (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² using area tiles and cut-out squares
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: area models and expanding brackets to get an x² term
lessonMap.usesData: Squares 12² = (10 + 2)² = 144, 8² = (10 − 2)² = 64 and 10² = 100 tested against the plot widths; Model v1 of area models

lessonMap.focus: Difference of two squares and applying identities
lessonMap.teaches: Derive a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) by cutting a small square from a large square and rearranging, and use it for quick mental calculation
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 and 2: area models of squares and the two square identities
lessonMap.usesData: 52² − 48² = 4 × 100 = 400; area-model link: 100 − (x − 10)² = x(20 − x), previewed only (full use in L8); model revised with all three identities

lessonMap.teaches: Factorise x² + bx + c by finding two numbers whose sum is b and whose product is c, and check with tiles or expansion
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 and 2: expansion (x + p)(x + q) = x² + (p + q)x + pq run in reverse; area tiles
lessonMap.usesData: x² + 8x + 15 = (x + 3)(x + 5) from L1; x² − 20x + 96 = (x − 8)(x − 12) because the numbers −8 and −12 have sum −20 and product 96, linking back to the 8 m and 12 m plots

lessonMap.focus: Factorising ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 1) and special cases
lessonMap.teaches: Factorise ax² + bx + c where a ≠ 1 using the grouping method (split the middle term using numbers with product ac) and the area-tile method, and compare methods
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 4: sum-and-product factorising; Lessons 2 and 3: recognising perfect squares and difference of two squares as special cases
lessonMap.usesData: 2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3) (ac = 6, split 6x and x); special cases x² + 10x + 25 and x² − 100; DQB review of which methods work best

lessonMap.teaches: Use the zero-product property to solve a quadratic equation written as a product equal to zero, and interpret both solutions
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 4 and 5: factorising; Lesson 1: the area expression x(20 − x)
lessonMap.usesData: x(20 − x) = 96, so x² − 20x + 96 = 0, (x − 8)(x − 12) = 0, x = 8 or x = 12 (the same 8 m by 12 m plot turned round); resolves the central puzzle; model revised to include two solutions

lessonMap.focus: Forming and solving equations from real-life situations
lessonMap.teaches: Translate a worded situation into a quadratic equation (define the variable, write the equation, rearrange to zero) and reject solutions that do not fit the context
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 6: solving by factorisation and checking solutions; Lessons 1 and 4: forming expressions from areas
lessonMap.usesData: Mandazi tray x(x + 4) = 60 giving x = 6 (reject −10); path around 12 m by 8 m shamba (12 + 2w)(8 + 2w) = 140 giving w = 1 (reject −11); thrown ball h = 20t − 5t², h = 15 gives t = 1 and t = 3, both valid

lessonMap.focus: Applying and synthesising: design a school-garden plot
lessonMap.teaches: Combine forming, factorising and solving to design and justify a plot for a target area and fence length, and explain the maximum area using A = 100 − (x − 10)²
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 to 7: forming expressions, the three identities, factorisation, two solutions, rejecting invalid ones
lessonMap.usesData: Design example 40 m fence and 84 m² gives x² − 20x + 84 = 0, so a 6 m by 14 m plot; 105 m² impossible because the maximum is 100 m² at x = 10; the full area table; final DQB and final cumulative model
